title: Comparative advantage: why trade helps even the best
examples: Why trade if you are better at everything?

explain.say: Amara and Leo are running a school fair stall selling cakes and cards. Amara is faster at making both! So should she do all the work? Look at the board: how long each of them takes.

draw.text: Comparative advantage: why trade helps even the best

explain.say: See Amara's side light up? She bakes a cake in 1 hour and makes a card in 2 hours. Leo needs 3 hours for either. Being better at both is called absolute advantage. So, does Amara need Leo at all?

Look closely at Leo. For Amara, one card costs the time of 2 cakes. For Leo, one card costs the time of just 1 cake. So cards cost Leo less in what he gives up. That is comparative advantage. Can you see why Leo should make cards?

Let's test it. Amara has 3 hours and Leo has 6. If each makes one of both, together they get 2 cakes and 2 cards. If Amara only bakes and Leo only makes cards, they get 3 cakes and 2 cards. Look: one extra cake, same time!

Countries do this too: Bangladesh makes clothes, Chile mines copper, Japan builds cars, and they trade. Brilliant! Wow: David Ricardo explained this in 1817 using England, Portugal, cloth and wine, and it is still the heart of trade economics.

faq.a: You have a comparative advantage in something if you can make it at a lower opportunity cost than someone else, meaning you give up less to make it.
Absolute advantage means being able to make something faster or with fewer resources than someone else. Amara has an absolute advantage in both cakes and cards.
asks: What is the difference between absolute and comparative advantage?

faq.a: When each person or country focuses on what it gives up least to make, the same hours produce more in total. Then they trade so everyone gets a mix.
David Ricardo was a British economist who, in 1817, explained comparative advantage with an example of England and Portugal making cloth and wine.
Trade usually makes countries better off overall, but some workers lose out when cheaper imports replace their industry. Many economists say governments should help those workers retrain.

facts: David Ricardo set out comparative advantage in On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation (1817).
In the example, specialising turns 2 cakes and 2 cards into 3 cakes and 2 cards with the same 9 hours of work.

quiz.show: Amara takes 1 hour per cake and 2 per card; Leo takes 3 hours for each. Who should make the cards?
quiz.why: A card costs Leo 1 cake of time but costs Amara 2, so Leo has the comparative advantage.

wrong.2: Cards are wanted, and Leo can make them at the lowest opportunity cost.
